title: Cut marks on mammoth bones suggest Ice Age hunters killed the giants themselves
dek: New finds at a 30,000-year-old open-air site challenge the idea that early humans only scavenged ancient ivory. Cut marks point to active hunting and butchery.
body: More than 2,000 finds emerged from July and October 2026 excavations at Breitenbach-Schneidemühle in southern Saxony-Anhalt. Among them are mammoth bones, large tusk fragments and worked ivory. Most striking are cut marks on mammoth bones that indicate the carcasses were butchered. The site covers roughly 10,000 square metres and is the largest known open-air settlement of the Aurignacian culture in western Eurasia.

Earlier research had argued that the ivory worked at Breitenbach was significantly older than the human occupation, dated to roughly 32,000 to 34,000 years ago. That led researchers to think people collected fossil or subfossil ivory from the landscape rather than killing mammoths themselves. Dr Olaf Jöris of MONREPOS, part of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology, said previous investigations suggested the ivory was likely older than the settlement.

Animal remains from the site show inhabitants primarily hunted reindeer, with horses taken less often and red deer only occasionally. Foxes and hares were also exploited, probably for fur. The newly discovered mammoth remains with cut marks now suggest hunters may have killed mammoths at or near the site. Tusks would have supplied valuable ivory and hides may have been used for clothing or shelters.

Breitenbach is unusual because most Aurignacian sites are caves or rock shelters. Large well-preserved open-air settlements are rare. The scale lets archaeologists study how people organised living and working spaces. Dr Marcel Weiß of Saxony-Anhalt’s State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology called an open-air site of this size with such preservation very special.

Researchers have identified specialised activity areas across the settlement. These include zones for working mammoth ivory and processing Arctic fox and mountain hare pelts. An ivory workshop yielded large quantities of manufacturing debris alongside finished and partially finished objects such as perforated beads, projectile points and fragments of carved figurines. Ivory served for weapons, tools, jewellery and art.

The site was discovered in 1924 when a schoolboy found a mammoth tooth during sawmill construction. Swedish archaeologist Dr Nils Niklasson directed the first extensive excavations in 1927, investigating nearly 400 square metres. The 2026 mammoth concentrations are the first large bone finds since Niklasson’s work. Modern investigation resumed in 2009 through a joint project of MONREPOS and the State Office, with more than 150 additional square metres excavated using modern techniques.

The combination of exceptional preservation, specialised working areas and thousands of animal and artefact remains is allowing researchers to reconstruct daily life in unusual detail. The latest mammoth discoveries could add another dimension, suggesting people were not simply scavenging ancient ivory but may have confronted, killed and butchered mammoths themselves.
doesnt_show: The cut marks indicate butchery but do not yet confirm the mammoths were hunted rather than scavenged from recent natural deaths. Further analysis is needed to establish exactly how the animals died and how extensively they were exploited.
settle: Microscopic analysis of the cut marks and stable isotope studies of the bones would clarify whether the mammoths were freshly killed and how often they were hunted.
